title: Bars, beats, and the grid
summary: 4/4, bars, beats and 16th steps, and why moving the snare to beat 3 makes the trap bounce.

steps.title: Count it: bars, beats, steps
steps.body:
Nearly every hip hop beat is in **4/4**: four beats per bar. Count it out loud: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4. Each group of four is one **bar**.

The drum grid splits every beat into four **16th steps**, so one bar is 16 steps. Count them "1 e & a, 2 e & a, 3 e & a, 4 e & a".

The beats sit on steps **1, 5, 9 and 13**. Those are your landmarks.

Where the snare goes decides the feel. Snare on beats 2 and 4 is the normal backbeat. Snare only on beat 3 is **half-time**, the slow, heavy trap bounce.
steps.deeper:
**4/4** means four beats per bar, with a quarter note as the beat. An **8th note** is half a beat (8 per bar) and a **16th note** is a quarter of a beat (16 per bar). Beat n starts on step 4 × (n − 1) + 1.

In normal time the snare hits beats 2 and 4. That's the **backbeat**.

In **half-time** the snare moves to beat 3 only. It hits half as often, so the groove feels half as fast even though the BPM hasn't changed: 140 BPM in half-time nods like 70. The long gap between snares leaves room for a rapper to ride, while fast hats on top keep the energy up.

steps.title: Normal time vs half-time
steps.caption: Both are 140 BPM with the same kick and hats. Only the snare moves.

examples.label: Snare on 2 and 4
examples.explanation: The normal backbeat. Two snares per bar, so it feels quick: your head nods at 140.

examples.label: Snare on 3 (half-time)
examples.explanation: One snare per bar. Same BPM, but your head nods half as fast, like 70. This is the trap bounce.

steps.title: Slow snare, fast hats
steps.body:
Half-time slows the snare down. The hats are how trap puts the speed back.

Over a half-time snare, hats on each beat feel heavy and empty. Hats in fast **16ths** feel urgent, even though the snare hasn't moved. Add quick rolls and you've got the signature trap sound: a slow nod with a fast top.

That contrast is the point. The snare sets the speed your head nods at. The hats set the energy.
steps.deeper:
At 140 BPM one 16th step lasts about 0.11 seconds (60 ÷ 140 ÷ 4).

In half-time the felt beat is 70 BPM, and against that slow beat, 16th hats at 140 move as fast as 32nd notes would at 70. That's where the feeling of fast hats over a slow snare comes from.

A **roll** packs in hits faster than the grid: 2 per step (32nd notes), 4 per step (64th notes), or 3 spread across 2 steps (16th-note triplets). Right before a snare, or at the end of a bar, a roll pushes the groove forward into what comes next.

steps.title: Slow hats vs fast hats
steps.caption: The same 140 BPM half-time kick and snare in all three. Only the hats change.

examples.label: Hats on the beat
examples.explanation: One hat per beat. It sits with the slow half-time feel: heavy, spacious, almost sleepy.

examples.label: 16th-note hats
examples.explanation: Four hats per beat: fast hats over a slow snare. Same groove underneath, much more urgency.

examples.label: 16ths with rolls
examples.explanation: The same 16ths, plus a 16th-note triplet roll into the snare in bar 1 and a 32nd-to-64th roll at the end of bar 2. This is the trap top end.

steps.title: Build a half-time skeleton
steps.prompt:
Put a **kick on beat 1** (step 1) and a **snare on beat 3** (step 9) in every bar. Switch bars with the bar picker, or use **Copy to next**.

Hats are up to you. Try 8ths, then 16ths, and hear the energy change. Press play while you work.
hints: Beats land on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13. Beat 3 is step 9, the first step of the second half of the bar.
The check listens to the **snare row (SNR)**, not the clap. Put the beat 3 hit in that row.
Every bar counts. Pick Bar 1, tap step 1 on the kick and step 9 on the snare, then tap **Copy to next**.

steps.message: Nice. This one was practice, so nothing from the grid goes into Your Track. You'll build the real drums in Drums & groove.
